text: Do you think this is justice, when you say, "I am in the right, not God"?
For you ask, "What good does it do me? What do I gain by not sinning?"* [*Or "What advantage is it to you?"—the Hebrew has "to you," which may address God.]

versions.text: For you ask, "What good does it do me? What do I gain by not sinning?"
versions.explanation: The Hebrew לָךְ is second person ("to you"), so the first line may be Job's question directed at God rather than about his own benefit. A brief footnote preserves the recognized ambiguity without changing the readable main text.

text: I will answer you—you and your friends with you.
Look up at the heavens and see; gaze at the clouds so high above you.
If you sin, how does that harm him? If your offenses pile up, what does it do to him?
If you are righteous, what do you give him? Or what does he receive from your hand?

versions.text: If you are righteous, what have you given him? What does he receive from your hand?
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb תִּתֶּן is imperfect, parallel to יִקָּח ("does he receive"), which the second clause already renders as present. "What have you given him" shifts to a completed past action and breaks the parallel rhythm of the couplet.

versions.text: If you are righteous, what do you give him? What does he receive from your hand?
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has the connective אוֹ ("or") joining the two questions, which ties the couplet together and heightens the rhetorical force. Restoring it also reads well aloud, since the second question then flows from the first rather than standing as a separate assertion.

text: Your wickedness affects only a man like yourself, and your righteousness only a human being.
People cry out under the weight of oppression; they plead for relief from the arm of the mighty.
But no one asks, "Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night,
who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth and makes us wiser than the birds of the sky?"
There they cry out, but he gives no answer, because of the arrogance of the wicked.
Surely God does not listen to empty talk; the Almighty pays it no regard.
How much less, then, when you say he takes no notice! Yet your case lies before him—so wait for him.
And now, because his anger has not brought punishment, and he takes little note of wrongdoing,

versions.text: And now, because his anger has not punished, because he seems to take little note of wrongdoing,
versions.explanation: "His anger has not punished" is awkward English (anger is not normally the agent of punishing), and "he seems to" adds a hedge not present in the Hebrew. The revision keeps the sense while reading more smoothly aloud and repeating "because" only once.

text: Job opens his mouth with empty words and multiplies talk without knowledge.
